## 1. Identification Strategy  

Method: Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), interpreted as a *fuzzy* RD when the ultimate implementation of the proposal is the outcome, and as a *sharp* RD when the passage itself is the treatment.  

Justification  
•	The institutional rule “> 50 % of votes cast ⇒ proposal passes” creates a mechanical, discontinuous jump in the probability that the proposal is deemed approved.  
•	Proposals that win 49 % vs. 51 % of the vote should be quasi-randomly assigned because small changes in individual votes or last-minute broker votes determine the outcome.  
•	Therefore, firms just above the 50 % cutoff provide a valid counterfactual for firms just below the cutoff.  
•	RDD exploits exactly this local randomization, requires no panel pre-trends, and fits the cross-sectional nature of voting outcomes.  

We will estimate:  

(a) ITT: effect of *passage* on same-day and post-meeting stock returns, governance indices, etc. (sharp RD).  
(b) LATE: effect of *actual implementation* on outcomes, using passage as instrument (fuzzy RD/2SLS in a narrow bandwidth).  

## 2. Treatment and Control Definition  

•	Running variable:  
 VoteShareᵢ = percentage of votes cast in favor of proposal i.  

•	Cutoff: 50 %.  
 Centered running variable: mᵢ = VoteShareᵢ – 0.5.  

•	Treatment indicator (sharp specification):  
 Passᵢ = 1{VoteShareᵢ ≥ 0.5}.  

•	Control group: proposals with 45 %–49.999 % support in the main (±5 pp) window.  

•	Treatment timing / event date: the annual meeting date at which the vote occurs.  
 – For event-study style CARs, day 0 = meeting date.  
 – For accounting variables, fiscal year t is the year that contains the meeting. Outcomes can be measured in t+1, t+2, etc.  

•	Fuzzy component (actual implementation):  
 Implementᵢt = 1 if the governance provision is fully put in place within two years after the vote.  
 2SLS first stage: Implementᵢt ← Passᵢ + f(mᵢ) + …  

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1.	Continuity of potential outcomes at the 50 % cutoff (no other determinants jump exactly at 50 %).  
 Plausibility: firms cannot perfectly predict the exact final vote share; minute-by-minute trading or abstentions generate noise.  

A2.	No precise manipulation of the running variable (no “bunching” just above 50 %).  
 Plausibility: while management can campaign, it is difficult to engineer *exactly* 50.000 % of the vote. McCrary density tests will assess this.  

A3.	Local common shocks: any news other than the proposal outcome arriving on meeting day is smoothly distributed around 50 %.  
 Plausibility: multiple proposals on the same ballot are typically voted on together; we will control for other proposals in the same meeting.  

A4.	Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): a proposal’s passage at firm A does not directly affect the return of a firm B in the bandwidth.  
 Plausibility: unlikely that narrowly passing at A immediately moves B’s price unless they are peers with simultaneous meetings; peer effects can be checked.  

## 4. Main Threats and Mitigation  

T1.	Manipulation / vote buying near 50 %.  
 – McCrary (2008) density test on the centered vote share.  
 – Balance checks of pre-determined covariates (size, prior returns, governance index) within the chosen bandwidth.  
 – Re-estimate with even tighter windows (±2 pp) where manipulation is nearly impossible.  

T2.	Multiple contemporaneous proposals or confounding events at the same meeting.  
 – Include meeting-level fixed effects when more than one close governance proposal is on the ballot, or keep only the *closest* proposal per meeting for a leave-one-out robustness check.  

T3.	Non-compliance (passage does not always lead to actual implementation).  
 – Report ITT (policy effect of passage) and 2SLS/LATE (effect of implementation).  
 – Document first-stage strength (F-stat > 10) and implementation rates above/below 50 %.  

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # general purpose OLS/2SLS
library(rdrobust)     # RD inference
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge data
# ---------------------------------------------------
iss   <- fread("iss_votes_1997_2007.csv")          # proposal-level
crsp  <- fread("crsp_daily_returns.csv")           # firm-date
comp  <- fread("compustat_fundamentals.csv")       # firm-year
gov   <- fread("governance_measures.csv")          # firm-year

# merge ISS with Compustat gvkey information
iss <- merge(iss, comp[, .(gvkey, year, assets = at, roa = roat, lev = dltt/at, q = tq)], 
             by = c("gvkey", "year"), all.x = TRUE)

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# ---------------------------------------------------
iss[, vote_share  := votes_for / (votes_for + votes_against)]
iss[, margin      := vote_share - 0.5]                    # running variable
iss[, pass        := as.integer(vote_share >= 0.5)]
iss[, abs_margin  := abs(margin)]
bandwidth <- 0.05                                         # 5 percentage points

# restrict to main bandwidth
main_sample <- iss[abs_margin <= bandwidth]

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main RD estimate – sharp ITT
# ---------------------------------------------------
rd_out <- rdrobust(y = main_sample$CAR_[-1,1],     # e.g., CAR[-1,+1]
                   x = main_sample$margin)

print(rd_out)       # local linear, robust bias-corrected estimate

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 4. Fuzzy RD / 2SLS: implementation as outcome
# ---------------------------------------------------
main_sample[, implement := as.integer(implemented_within2yr == 1)]

# first stage
fs <- feols(implement ~ pass + poly(margin,1) | 0, data = main_sample)
summary(fs)

# second stage (2SLS): effect on outcome, e.g., change in board independence
fuzzy <- feols(board_indep_change ~ 1 | pass + poly(margin,1),      # fixest syntax: y ~ 1 | endogenous | instruments
               endog = ~ implement,
               inst =  ~ pass,
               data  = main_sample)
summary(fuzzy)

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 5. Covariate balance check
# ---------------------------------------------------
covs <- c("assets","roa","lev","q","board_size")
balance <- lapply(covs, function(v){
  feols(as.formula(paste0(v," ~ pass + margin")), data = main_sample)
})
lapply(balance, summary)

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: different bandwidths
# ---------------------------------------------------
for(bw in c(0.03, 0.02)){
  tmp <- main_sample[abs_margin <= bw]
  print(paste("Bandwidth:", bw))
  print(rdrobust(tmp$CAR_[-1,1], tmp$margin)$coef)
}

# ---------------------------------------------------
# 7. Manipulation test
# ---------------------------------------------------
rdplotdensity(main_sample$margin, c = 0)  # visual
rddensity(main_sample$margin, c = 0)      # numerical McCrary test
```

(Variables such as `CAR_[-1,1]` are assumed to have been pre-computed from CRSP daily returns.)

## 6. Expected Results (Prior)  

Governance proposals that pass narrowly should on average raise firm value because they curb managerial entrenchment. I expect:  
•	Event-window CAR of roughly +1 % to +1.5 % for a 3-day window around the meeting for the marginal winner versus marginal loser.  
•	Within two years, a 5–10 pp increase in board independence and ~0.05–0.1 improvement in Tobin’s Q (scaled by pre-vote mean of ~1.8).  
Larger effects for poison-pill removal and board de-classification; smaller for advisory say-on-pay.  

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  

C1.	No manipulation of running variable: 1  
C2.	Continuity of baseline covariates at cutoff: 1  
C3.	Correct bandwidth / functional form and robust bias correction: 1  
C4.	No other discontinuities at 50 % from simultaneous policies: 0 (some risk from multiple proposals)  
C5.	Sufficient data density for precise estimates: 1  

Total: 4/5 – overall strong but must rule out confounding multiple-proposal meetings.
